en: Magma rising beneath Mayon Volcano heats groundwater, creating steam pressure that eventually triggers explosive volcanic eruptions.
Warm ocean waters in the Philippine Sea evaporate and rise, fueling the strong winds and heavy rains of typhoons.
The Cagayan River carries eroded soil downstream, depositing sediment to build a wide delta where it meets the Babuyan Channel.
Slightly acidic rainwater dissolves the limestone bedrock of the Puerto Princesa Subterranean River, slowly carving out massive underground cave systems.
Warm, shallow, sunlit waters around Tubbataha Reefs allow photosynthetic algae inside coral polyps to thrive and build massive reef structures.
The southwest monsoon pushes moisture-laden winds from the Indian Ocean across the Philippines, causing heavy rainfall during the summer months.
Underground magma heats groundwater in the Tiwi geothermal field, producing steam that spins turbines to generate renewable electricity.
The collision of the Philippine Sea Plate and the Eurasian Plate pushes the earth upward, forming the Sierra Madre mountains.
Taal Volcano's past explosive eruptions collapsed its magma chamber, creating a large caldera that later filled with water to form Taal Lake.
Deforestation on steep slopes removes tree roots that hold soil, causing heavy rains to trigger deadly landslides in mountainous Philippine provinces.
The gravitational pull of the moon creates strong tidal currents in the San Bernardino Strait, driving massive ocean volumes through the narrow passage.
Dense mangrove roots along the coast of Palawan trap moving sediment, stabilizing the shoreline and protecting inland areas from storm surges.
